name: DunedinPACE testing

lead: DunedinPACE is a DNA methylation biomarker, published in eLife in 2022, that estimates the pace of biological aging from a blood sample. A score near 1 means aging about one biological year per calendar year; higher scores suggest faster aging. Consumer and research services offer it, and longevity-focused biohackers use it as a progress dashboard.

For appearance, the appeal is indirect: people hope that habits that slow the score, such as exercise, diet, sleep and not smoking, also support a younger-looking face and body over time. Randomised trials have begun testing whether interventions such as exercise, supplements and calorie restriction shift epigenetic clock scores, with varied findings.

paras: A user provides a blood (or sometimes saliva) sample through a lab or a commercial service, which runs a methylation array and returns a score. Some retest after months of a new diet, training or supplement routine to see whether the score changes. Because the test is read alongside other markers, it is often kept in a broader biomarker-tracking log.

The test itself involves an ordinary blood draw or sample collection. The main concerns discussed by researchers are interpretation: epigenetic clocks are validated at population level, an individual score has measurement noise, and it is not fully established what the scores represent or whether changing them changes health outcomes. Genetic-data privacy is also a consideration when using commercial labs.

chain: Adjust lifestyle and retest to track progress toward slower aging and a younger-looking trajectory
angle.text: DunedinPACE does not change appearance; it measures an aging-rate estimate that users track while changing habits. Those habits (training, diet, sleep, not smoking) are the ones people link to a younger look.

lead: DunedinPACE is a blood-based DNA methylation biomarker of the pace of aging, introduced in a 2022 paper in eLife [1]. Unlike earlier epigenetic clocks that estimate a person's biological age in years, it estimates a rate: roughly how many years of biological aging a person accumulates per calendar year. Testing services now offer it to consumers and researchers.

People interested in looksmaxxing and longevity use pace-of-aging tests as a tracking tool. The reasoning is that habits associated with slower measured aging, such as regular exercise, a nutritious diet, adequate sleep and avoiding smoking, may also support a youthful appearance over the long term, so a falling score serves as feedback that routines are working. Whether a pace-of-aging score tracks visible aging directly has not been established.

Research on epigenetic clocks is extensive and includes randomised trials of exercise, supplements, diet and calorie restriction on clock outcomes, as well as observational studies linking scores to education, childhood adversity, alcohol dependence, musculoskeletal disease and dementia [2][3][4][5][6][7][8][9].

About 1 year of biological aging per calendar year

paras: Epigenetic clocks are analytical methods that use DNA methylation patterns as a biomarker of aging [10]. Horvath's multi-tissue clock, the first of its kind, used 353 CpG sites, with a median error of about 3.6 years [10]. Later generations such as PhenoAge and GrimAge incorporated clinical and environmental factors, with GrimAge described as especially strong in predicting mortality [10].

DunedinPACE is a methylation biomarker of the pace of aging rather than of age itself [1]. A higher score indicates faster aging relative to the reference pace. It is typically described as a second- or later-generation clock.

sections.h: Use in longevity and looksmaxxing communities
paras: In longevity circles, a pace-of-aging test is used as a periodic checkpoint, often alongside other biomarkers, to see whether a new routine coincides with a lower score. Looksmaxxing participants who adopt the practice tend to frame it as a way to monitor long-term skin, body and vitality maintenance rather than as an appearance treatment.

Researchers note that it is unclear what DNA methylation age actually measures, that predicting mortality does not establish causation, that clocks tend to underestimate age in older individuals, and that lifestyle factors have only weak associations with age acceleration in blood [10]. A systematic analysis of epigenetic age acceleration across 25 countries and 31 ethnicities examined how clocks extrapolate to different populations and tissue types [4].

Several randomised trials have measured methylation clocks as outcomes. In the DO-HEALTH trial, a post hoc analysis of 777 participants examined vitamin D, omega-3 and a home exercise program on four next-generation DNA methylation measures of aging [5]. The COSMOS trial evaluated 2-year effects of a multivitamin-multimineral and cocoa extract on five methylation measures [6]. The CALERIE trial studied long-term caloric restriction on methylation measures in healthy adults [7], and the DIRECT PLUS trial tested polyphenols on methylation-assessed biological age [8].

Observational studies have linked pace-of-aging scores to cognitive impairment and dementia [9], and a meta-analysis examined educational attainment and pace of aging [3]. Other studies connect accelerated epigenetic aging to alcohol dependence [11] and adverse childhood experiences [12]. No study cited here tests whether a DunedinPACE score tracks visible facial or skin aging.

timeline.event: Horvath's multi-tissue epigenetic clock is the first of its type [10].
CALERIE trial reports calorie restriction effects on methylation measures [7].
DO-HEALTH analysis of vitamin D, omega-3 and exercise on methylation clocks appears in Nature Aging [5].
